TOKEN HEADER IS OUR CHOICE, NOT THE SPEC'S: the A2A specification defines PushNotificationConfig.token as a field but names NO HTTP header to carry it (https://a2a-protocol.org/latest/topics/streaming-and-async/, fetched 2026-07-26). What is delivered is an A2A StreamResponse payload with an APPLICATION-SPECIFIC token header (X-A2A-Notification-Token) — it is NOT "spec-compliant push", and a foreign peer expecting a different header simply will not see the token. Every delivery proof in this case ran against a LOOPBACK sink this repo wrote; a loopback sink is not interop, so a foreign peer accepting these deliveries remains §6 leg 2 and `a2a` stays preview

D12 PARTIALLY CLOSED — OWNERSHIP VERIFICATION IS ABSENT: the contract names domain allowlisting, ownership verification AND an egress firewall. The allowlist (normalized whole-host equality) and the firewall (packages/egress + the pinned dialer, with redirects REVALIDATED per hop) are implemented and RED-proven; nothing verifies that the client registering a webhook target actually controls it. A deployment exposed to untrusted registrants must set PushPolicy.AllowedHosts — when it is empty the egress policy alone governs, and any public https host a client names will be POSTed to

DELIVERY IS NOT DURABLE AND NOT OBSERVER-DRIVEN: the pending set is IN-PROCESS, so a crash between accepting a notification and delivering it drops that notification — the retry/dead-letter discipline is the webhook pump's, but the queue behind it is not. Delivery fires only on the state-producing operations the server itself serves (message:send, message:stream, tasks:subscribe, tasks:cancel); there is NO asynchronous observer of run terminality, so a run that reaches a terminal state with no A2A request in flight notifies nobody. Both gaps need durable per-target delivery state and therefore a migration, which E19 excludes by construction

NO REAL WORKSPACE: every Slack proof this case COUNTS runs against a FAKE peer — a fixture that signs the way the verification page documents, a local HTTP server standing in for slack.com/api, and a fake WSS server built from the Socket Mode page. The shipped routes (events + interactivity), the Socket Mode connect loop, and the decision chain are exercised end to end over real Postgres, but nothing here is a receipt from a real workspace: no test that runs WITHOUT credentials opens a socket to slack.com. That receipt is §6 leg 1 and is what caps `slack` at preview — and Socket Mode is the cheapest way to collect it, since it needs no public URL

ONE SOCKET MODE CONNECTION, ONE WORKSPACE: the connect loop is proven with a SINGLE connection to the single workspace PALAI_SLACK_SOCKET_TEAM_ID names. Multi-workspace fan-out (N connections = N sockets) is NOT built — a listing query, per-connection supervision and add/remove on registration are connection-pool management, i.e. scale work. Two consequences a reader should not have to infer: a deployment serving several workspaces runs Socket Mode for at most one of them, and a workspace registered AFTER the control plane boots is not picked up until it restarts

AN ACKNOWLEDGED ENVELOPE WHOSE ADMISSION THEN FAILS IS LOST, and this is an asymmetry with the HTTP transport rather than a shared property: the HTTP route acknowledges AFTER the reservation commits, so a failure there earns a Slack redelivery. Socket Mode publishes no acknowledgement budget at all (the 3-second figure is documented for the HTTP callback and for interactivity, not for an envelope), so the loop answers FIRST — which satisfies any budget that may exist, at the cost that Slack will not redeliver an envelope it has seen acknowledged. A failing admission is therefore logged as a named loss and produces no run

NO RESPONSE PAYLOAD IS EVER SENT ON AN ACKNOWLEDGEMENT: accepts_response_payload is decoded and slack.SocketAck refuses a payload on an envelope declaring false — the documented rule, enforced as a typed error rather than a silent drop — but nothing in-process has anything to say back inside an acknowledgement (an admitted run answers later, in the thread). The accepting branch is therefore exercised by the rule's own unit test, not by a real sender

THE APPROVAL MESSAGE IS NOT POSTED BY ANYTHING IN-PROCESS: the decision path REPAIRS the message a click arrived on (chat.update, bot token from bot_token_ref, per-channel Special-Tier pacing, one bounded 429 repair) and records its ts as the thread's repair handle. What posts an approval message with its two minted buttons in the first place is the credential-gated live leg (tests/live/slack) and, later, whatever composes approval UX — there is no in-process worker that fans approval messages out. Block Kit construction here is deliberately minimal (two buttons + the authoritative detail); a rich approval UI is the console's job. Enterprise Grid / org-wide install is out of scope: the interactivity route never resolves an enterprise id

NO FEEDBACK TO AN UNAUTHORIZED CLICKER: a refused decision answers Slack 200 with nothing done and is recorded control-plane-side only, so the clicking user sees no reply at all. Telling them would need an ephemeral message (response_url, whose 30-minute/5-use window is the wrong tool for approval repair, or chat.postEphemeral); that is deliberately not built

TERMINAL-SUMMARY MEASUREMENT: the proof's terminal_summary_posts counts the terminal SURFACE posts (exactly one repaired chat.update, never duplicated). The §63.3 fan-out form — one terminal summary per delivery id, with two canonical deliveries — is NOT asserted: there is no shipped Slack outbound worker to fan out, so a second post would be fixture theatre rather than evidence

JOURNEY STEP 8 IS COMMAND-ACCEPTANCE: the change_config route switch is asserted DURABLE (the row reads back queued on the session, carrying the new model), not APPLIED — applying a boundary config change needs a running engine, which this journey does not start, so that is an E08 execution-tier proof (apps/control-plane/internal/execution). Step 9's cancellation IS asserted to a real terminal: the §9.2 interrupt-delivery message reads back queued for the pump AND the run is driven to `canceled` through the production CancelRunReconciled path (§26.10/SES-010), with the run row re-read. a delivery without a 2xx inside 3 seconds is retried three times (immediately, +1m, +5m); a non-200 answer carrying `x-slack-no-retry: 1` suppresses the retry, so a TERMINAL rejection must set it or a poison event is pulled four times
a retry carries both `x-slack-retry-num` (1..3) and `x-slack-retry-reason` (http_timeout, http_error, connection_failed, ssl_error, too_many_redirects, unknown_error)
event_id is globally unique across workspaces; that a RETRY repeats the same event_id is NOT stated on the page and is carried in the tree as a labelled ASSUMPTION the live leg asserts
the v0 base string is exactly 'v0:'+timestamp+':'+raw_body, HMAC-SHA256 hex, the header value 'v0='-prefixed, compared timing-safe, with a timestamp more than five minutes old refused

an interaction arrives application/x-www-form-urlencoded with the JSON in a single `payload` parameter and must be answered 200 within 3 seconds; the signature is verified over the RAW form body BEFORE `payload` is extracted
chat.postMessage is Special Tier — roughly one message per channel per second with short bursts — and a throttled call answers 429 with Retry-After in seconds

every envelope must be acknowledged so Slack knows whether to retry; NO ack-time budget and no retry count are published for Socket Mode (the 3-second rule is the HTTP page's), so the tree acknowledges BEFORE the work and names the gap rather than inventing an SLA

apps.connections.open returns a short-lived wss ticket URL; a `disconnect` with reason `warning` arrives ~10 seconds before close, and up to 10 concurrent connections are supported — so a graceful refresh OVERLAPS a new socket before draining the old one
the envelope carries `accepts_response_payload`; a response payload may only be returned on an envelope that accepts one
Socket Mode envelopes are NOT signed — the pre-authenticated WebSocket is the authentication — so the absence of a v0 verify on this transport is the documented behaviour, not an omission

the server POSTs a StreamResponse (task | message | statusUpdate | artifactUpdate), not a full Task; PushNotificationConfig.token exists for client-side validation but the spec names NO header to carry it, so our header choice cannot be called spec-compliant
a server SHOULD NOT blindly POST to any client-supplied URL: allowlist the domain, verify ownership, and put an egress firewall in front of it

contracts.requirement: `features.agent_view` is the CURRENT surface and `assistant_view` is legacy: new apps can only use the Agent messaging experience, and switching from `assistant_view` to `agent_view` CANNOT be reversed

`agent_view` carries `agent_description` (required, at most 300 characters) plus optional `actions[]` and `suggested_prompts[]`, and the suggested prompts have a STATIC manifest form that costs no API call at all

the scopes SPLIT by method: assistant.threads.setStatus and the whole chat.startStream/appendStream/stopStream family need `chat:write`, while `assistant:write` is only for setSuggestedPrompts and setTitle — so streaming and status need NO new scope
`message.im` REQUIRES the `im:history` scope — it is the only way to receive it — which reverses E19's explicit decision not to grant standing read access to the bot's DMs
`app_home_opened` requires NO scope and carries a `tab` of `home` or `messages`; the panel is the `messages` tab and neither tab is a conversation

`app_context` is delivered INSIDE the `message.im` and `app_home_opened` payloads, each entity being {type, value, team_id} in relevance order, so no server-side context state is needed and `app_context_changed` is only a refresh signal
`assistant_thread_started` / `assistant_thread_context_changed` belong to the LEGACY `assistant_view` only — a deprecated surface is not built upon, and the tree subscribes to neither
chat.startStream is Tier 2 (20+/min) while chat.appendStream is Tier 4 (100+/min) — starting a stream is FIVE TIMES scarcer than appending to one — and markdown_text is capped at 12,000 characters

`recipient_user_id` and `recipient_team_id` are REQUIRED when streaming to channels; what the other channel members see while a stream is open is NOT stated, so the claim is only "a stream for the asker, a terminal message for everyone"

a task card carries {task_id, title, status, details} and Slack's status vocabulary is pending|in_progress|complete|error, which does NOT overlap ours — so an unmapped status must fail closed rather than be invented; chat.startStream's `task_display_mode` is `timeline` (default), `plan` or `dense`, and both arrived in the 2026-02-11 task-card release
chat.appendStream can answer `stopped_by_user` — the human stopped the STREAM from Slack's UI. It carries no authenticated actor, so it stops the stream and never the run

TWO SLACK PAGES CONTRADICT EACH OTHER on whether chat.appendStream accepts blocks (the guide says stopStream only; the method reference documents a `blocks` chunk type). An unresolved vendor contradiction is not a design freedom: blocks travel on chat.stopStream ONLY

a video block's `video_url` must be HTTPS, match one of the app's existing unfurl domains, answer 2xx, be publicly accessible and iframe-embeddable — so a Slack-hosted file can NEVER be a video block, and `links.embed:write` is therefore not requested

the `file` block is `source: "remote"` only and cannot be added to app surfaces directly; a real upload is files.getUploadURLExternal → POST → files.completeUploadExternal under a NEW `files:write` scope, which E20 does not request and does not build

assistant.threads.setStatus takes an optional `loading_messages` of at most 10 rotating strings and allows 600 requests/min per app per team — far above everything else, so status updates are not paced; setSuggestedPrompts allows at most FOUR prompts
assistant.threads.setTitle REQUIRES channel_id + thread_ts + title, and `app_home_opened` carries NO thread_ts — so a panel open cannot name a thread and makes no outbound call at all
a block_actions payload carries NO conversation-type field (the `channel` object is {id, name} alone), so the CLICK path cannot tell a DM from a channel and an unverifiable scope is treated as unmet

NO SLACK PAGE AGREES ON THE FIELD NAME: the changelog says `app_context`, the agents guide says `context` for app_home_opened, and message.im's example payload shows neither — so the mapper reads BOTH names, because a context that never arrives looks exactly like a user looking at nothing

an entity's `value` is POLYMORPHIC — a channel_id is a string while a message_context is an object — so it is decoded as raw JSON and only `slack#/types/channel_id` is ever described; a typed string field would have made one person's message view reject every DM in the workspace

db_assertions: RELEASE-LEVEL entry, not a UAT case (it has no tests/uat/cases directory): "the model cannot mint an actionable element" is not a behaviour one case asserts, it is an observation over a whole journey's outbound traffic — the E19-WIRING / E17-TIER precedent

every counter here was MEASURED by apps/control-plane/internal/store TestAgentSurfaceJourney against REAL PostgreSQL and the shipped routes, in the SAME process that served them: three entrances (an HTTP callback, a Socket Mode envelope and a panel DM), five deliveries of three source events, three runs, three visible messages

the source event ids are read back out of the idempotency_records the SHARED Admit wrote, not out of the journey's own bookkeeping — only that admission writes those rows, so the count IS the evidence that the panel opened no second admission path

the CROWN claim is RE-DERIVED, never believed: the closing message's actual blocks travel in this proof and uat.SweepActionableElements recomputes the actionable-element count from those bytes, in Complete() AND independently in AgentSurfacePromoteGate. A bundle declaring zero over a closing message containing a button is refused by construction

the sweep is shown to DISCRIMINATE before it is trusted: pointed at interactions.go's ApprovalMessage it finds seven actionable nodes, and pointed at the renderer's output for a model answer that FORGES `{"type":"actions",…,"action_id":"palai_approve"}` it finds zero — the forgery arrives as characters in markdown_text, where a human reads it and nobody can press it

NO TIER ADVANCES: uat.AgentSurfacePromoteGate composes uat.WiringPromoteGate, which REFUSES any capability sitting higher than the committed integration-wiring-0.1.0 lineage's extensions-0.1.0 baseline. A wider surface is the LEAST earned moment for a tier — see the three refusal reasons in the tier_decision assertions below

TIER DECISION, ARGUED AND REFUSED ON THE RECORD (1/3): a real workspace IS connected and a real run DID complete on 2026-07-26 (gpt-4o-mini-2024-07-18, 316 in / 153 out), but that run left NO CAPTURED RECEIPT and SlackAgentSurfaceProof.Peer is structurally the literal "fake". Moving the tier first requires DESIGNING what a real receipt IS — a transcript from which a verifier can re-derive workspace id + event id + run id — and that design is the content of §6 leg 1 itself
TIER DECISION (2/3): that run demonstrated ONE claim (a mention births a run), not the eight of SLK-001..008 — and E20 adds four more, so the fraction of the surface it covers went DOWN, not up

TIER DECISION (3/3): E20 GROWS the surface. agent_view, streaming and task cards are Slack's newest surfaces (2026-07, 2025-10 and 2026-02 respectively) and the YOUNGEST fakes in this repository are built against them. Raising a tier in the epic that grows the surface most is exactly what this gate exists to prevent. E20's contribution to leg 1 is to make it BIGGER and CHEAPER — the leg's text now covers the panel, the stream and the render, and `make uat-agent-surface-live` reduces its execution to ONE command

FIVE REQUIREMENTS ARE NOT IN THE CONTRACT LEDGER AND THAT IS THE HONEST ANSWER: plan §3.5 S16 names five things the vendor documentation does not state (what an unstopped stream does, whether chat.update works on a streaming message, whether a Socket-Mode-only app may call the streaming Web API, what the video block's Events-API exception opens, and whether interactive elements render in the panel).
